prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat with corticosteroids: oral corticosteroids are strongly advised against and IV methylprednisolone is not recommended [EAN_PNS_2023].
Do not give IVIg directly after plasma exchange, and do not give a second IVIg course [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].
Avoid sedating medications that depress respiratory drive while respiratory function is falling.
Do not start IVIg without checking renal function.
Do not use succinylcholine if intubation is needed: denervated muscle risks severe hyperkalaemia.
required_recommendations: Admit to ICU-level monitoring: FVC 58% predicted (below 60%) and MIP -28 cmH2O (weaker than -30 cmH2O), with bulbar weakness (dysphagia for thin liquids, nasal speech) and a weak cough.

Repeat FVC, MIP and MEP every 4 to 6 hours with checks of bulbar function, cough, secretions and fatigue; plan elective intubation if FVC falls below 20 mL/kg (about 1.35 L at 67.5 kg) or by more than 30%, MEP falls below 40 cmH2O, or bulbar function, cough or secretions worsen; intubate at once for respiratory distress, hypoxaemia or hypercapnia [Lawn_2001, EAN_PNS_2023].
Start IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total, about 27 g/day at 67.5 kg) or plasma exchange 200-250 mL/kg over 5 sessions: he cannot walk unaided and is 10 days from onset [EAN_PNS_2023].
Continuous cardiac telemetry with blood pressure monitoring for autonomic instability while weakness progresses.
Formal swallow assessment before any oral intake (dysphagia for thin liquids); keep nil by mouth or texture-modified until assessed.
Start mechanical / pharmacologic DVT prophylaxis appropriate for an immobilised inpatient.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy) after an upper respiratory infection

differential.key_features: Cannot be excluded at presentation: 10 days of progression fits GBS; reconsider if progression continues beyond 8 weeks or treatment-related fluctuations recur.
No sensory level or sphincter dysfunction; areflexia rather than hyperreflexia, facial diplegia, and a demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy on NCS.

differential.diagnosis: Acute polyradiculoneuropathy from Lyme / other infection
differential.key_features: No tick exposure or travel to an endemic area; CSF has no pleocytosis, whereas Lyme radiculitis gives a lymphocytic pleocytosis.
Pattern is ascending, not descending; sensory paresthesias prominent; EMG demyelinating, not low-amplitude with incremental RNS response.
Facial diplegia present but reflexes are preserved in MG; no fatigability pattern; EMG demyelinating.

key_clinical_evidence: Progressive, symmetric four-limb weakness with areflexia, facial diplegia and bulbar symptoms over 10 days after an upper respiratory infection, with CSF albuminocytological dissociation and a demyelinating NCS, meets Brighton level 1 [Brighton_2011].
CSF protein 78 mg/dL with 3 cells/mm3 is albuminocytological dissociation; a count above 50/mm3 would point to an infective or malignant polyradiculopathy.
The NCS pattern (prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction, absent F-waves) is consistent with a demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP).
Anti-ganglioside antibodies are not needed to diagnose typical GBS; anti-GQ1b is tested when Miller Fisher syndrome or an overlap is suspected [EAN_PNS_2023].

FVC 58% predicted (32.6 mL/kg) and MIP -28 cmH2O with bulbar weakness and a weak cough call for ICU-level monitoring; the intubation decision rests on the trend, bulbar function, cough, secretions and fatigue, not on one threshold [Lawn_2001, EAN_PNS_2023].

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A non-specific acute-phase response after the respiratory infection 3 weeks earlier; he is afebrile with no infective focus and the CSF has no pleocytosis or organisms, so no active infection explains the weakness.
red_herrings.data_point: Mild leukocytosis (WBC 11.2) with elevated CRP and ESR
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest active systemic infection or sepsis as the primary driver of weakness rather than post-infectious autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy.

interactions: Amlodipine with intravenous immunoglobulin: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction.
Amlodipine with plasma exchange: antihypertensives can add to procedure-related hypotension; relative caution, monitor blood pressure during exchanges.
general.summary: Current medication reviewed: amlodipine 5 mg once daily.
warnings: Dysautonomia in GBS causes blood pressure lability; review the need for antihypertensives against the measured blood pressure.

results.finding: Guidelines for adults with GBS who cannot walk unaided advise IVIg 2 g/kg over 5 days within 2 weeks of onset or plasma exchange within 4 weeks, with no preference between them; corticosteroids are not advised.
A second IVIg course in patients with a poor predicted prognosis did not improve outcome and caused more serious adverse events.

general.summary: IVIg or plasma exchange is advised for adults with GBS unable to walk unaided; neither is preferred, and a second IVIg course is not advised [EAN_PNS_2023, Walgaard_2021].

DML 8.1 ms (markedly prolonged); CV 28 m/s (severely reduced); CMAP 2.1 mV (significantly reduced)
Absent in bilateral median and peroneal nerves
Reduced recruitment of normal-morphology motor unit potentials in tibialis anterior and first dorsal interosseous bilaterally; no fibrillation potentials or positive sharp waves

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study and needle EMG. 1. Markedly prolonged distal motor latencies and reduced conduction velocities in bilateral median and peroneal motor nerves, with reduced right median and peroneal CMAP amplitudes. 2. Absent sural sensory nerve action potentials bilaterally. 3. Absent F-waves bilaterally in median and peroneal nerves, indicating proximal conduction failure. 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. 5. Reduced recruitment without active denervation on needle EMG. Electrophysiological pattern is consistent with an acquired demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.

quantitative_data.motor_CV_reduction: Median motor 22-27% below the lower limit of normal (49 m/s)

patient.chief_complaint: Ten-day progressive bilateral leg weakness, paresthesias, and facial diplegia with areflexia.

social_history.living_situation: Lives with wife and two children

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. H. is a 50-year-old man presenting to the emergency department with a 10-day history of progressive neurological symptoms. Approximately 3 weeks ago, he had a mild upper respiratory illness that resolved after 5 days. One week after recovery, he began noticing tingling in both feet. Over the following days, the tingling ascended to his knees and he developed progressive leg weakness — initially difficulty climbing stairs, then difficulty rising from a chair. By day 7, he noticed bilateral facial weakness and slurred speech. He presents today unable to walk without support. He has also noted dysphagia for thin liquids over the past 2 days and reports that his voice sounds 'nasal.' His wife noticed bilateral facial drooping which is now symmetric. He denies bladder dysfunction. He denies neck stiffness or fever. He has no history of tick exposure, recent travel, or toxin exposure. His symptoms have been progressive throughout with no fluctuation or improvement.

neurological_exam.additional: Respiratory: breathing comfortably at rest, no accessory muscle use or paradoxical abdominal movement. Cough weak.
neurological_exam.coordination: Cannot assess reliably due to weakness.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral facial weakness — forehead sparing absent (symmetric facial diplegia; upper and lower face involved). Dysarthria noted. Difficulty closing eyes fully bilaterally. All other cranial nerves intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Cannot stand without assistance. Too weak to attempt tandem gait.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. Anxious about his weakness.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 4/5, knee extension 4/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5 bilaterally. Upper extremity: shoulder abduction 4/5, wrist extension 4/5, grip 4/5 bilaterally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent deep tendon reflexes throughout: areflexia at bilateral biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral distal lower extremity paresthesias in a stocking distribution to the knees. Mild reduction in vibration at bilateral ankles.
